fields.question: Does calibration-aware RL score the entire explanation through its decision token?
fields.answer: No. It studies final-decision probability and calibration, not factual fidelity of all reasoning. Correct choices and credible probabilities require separate measurement.
fields.example: High probability for A doesn't make every preceding explanation step correct.

fields.question: How does local temperature calibration differ from full RLVR training?
fields.answer: Temperature rescales existing logits; full training changes the decision model. Shared calibration goals do not make postprocessing a full reproduction.
fields.example: A frozen model with tuned T uses no resampled trajectories or policy gradient.

fields.question: May calibration T be selected on test NLL?
fields.answer: No. Fit validation NLL, freeze, then report test accuracy and calibration. Choosing on test biases final evaluation. Local coverage is calibration and split isolation.
fields.example: Trying all temperatures on test and reporting the best overstates generalization.

fields.question: Why constrain decision probability if accuracy improves while ECE worsens?
fields.answer: Correctness only needs the top class right; calibration requires confidence to match actual hit frequency. RLVR can make correct choices overconfident. Measure separately, choose T on validation and reserve test. Post-hoc calibration is not full RL reproduction.
fields.example: Two models with identical labels can assign near-certainty or moderate confidence and differ in probability quality.

fields.question: Why consume each Online IcePop rollout batch once?
fields.answer: One update avoids extra staleness from reuse, making initial policy ratio one. Train/inference numerical correction remains.
fields.example: Discard the fresh batch after its update instead of optimizing against it again.

fields.question: Which correction does Online IcePop remove?
fields.answer: Remove reuse-induced stale-policy ratio and PPO clip, not the two-sided engine mask or original in-range ratio. Repeated updates invalidate the online simplification.
fields.example: Scheduling must enforce one use; deleting a line doesn't make training online.

fields.question: How verify Online IcePop never silently reuses a batch?
fields.answer: Track unique batch IDs and consumption; reject a second update. A local candidate group is only a scheduling proxy, not distributed rollout infrastructure.
fields.example: Retried delivery of the same batch is not fresh data.

fields.question: Why retain engine correction when Online IcePop updates only once?
fields.answer: Fresh one-use rollouts eliminate reuse staleness, so policy ratio at sampling is one and PPO clipping unnecessary. Equal weights can still produce different probabilities in training vs inference; IcePop keeps its two-sided mask and in-range ratio.
fields.example: A fresh answer can come from a lower-precision engine; freshness is not engine equality.

fields.question: Why model both train/inference mismatch and staleness in miniRL?
fields.answer: Equal weights may score differently across engines; old/new weights drift through learning. Separate them for appropriate on/off-policy correction.
fields.example: A kernel change and a policy update are distinct causes.

fields.question: What do MoE Routing Replay and ratio clipping address?
fields.answer: Replay restores expert execution paths; clipping limits update magnitude from probabilities. Clipping cannot reconstruct old routes.
fields.example: Saving which expert executed is different from lowering a large ratio.

fields.question: Does the local miniRL kernel prove distributed MoE stability?
fields.answer: No. It checks correction, clipping and routing state semantics. Real replay needs recorded token routes and actual aligned execution, not a label.
fields.example: A replay flag doesn't prove forward passes used the recorded experts.

fields.question: Why split engine mismatch and policy staleness, and where does routing replay help?
fields.answer: Numerical engine differences and weight drift are distinct. Correct on-policy probabilities, combine off-policy updates with clipping and replay rollout MoE routing to reduce path mismatch. Both probabilities and paths need testing; local kernels aren't a cluster.
fields.example: One token may route to different experts even with synchronized weights, which a stale-policy ratio does not fix.

fields.question: Why does IcePop mask very small train-to-serve ratios?
fields.answer: Upper clipping only controls huge weights; tiny ratios may also signal mismatch. A two-sided interval keeps trustworthy ratios without snapping others to boundaries.
fields.example: A training probability far below serving can be unreliable even though its weight is small.

fields.question: How do IcePop masking and TIS clipping treat out-of-range samples?
fields.answer: IcePop zeroes their gradient; TIS caps high weights but keeps them contributing. IcePop uses original in-range ratios, not ones.
fields.example: An oversized ratio can retain capped contribution in TIS but none in IcePop.

fields.question: Must IcePop distinguish engine ratio from policy ratio?
fields.answer: Yes. Engine ratio measures implementation mismatch; policy ratio measures current vs sampling policy. Mask the specified engine ratio only. No local real MoE/asynchronous system.
fields.example: Using model-learning drift as the engine mask could drop normal probability changes.

fields.question: How is zeroing out-of-range IcePop updates different from clipping to a boundary?
fields.answer: Clipping preserves boundary-weighted contribution; masking drops the current token gradient. IcePop uses two fixed bounds and original in-range correction. It filters mismatch, not text quality.
fields.example: Tiny ratio is unaffected by upper clipping, but two-sided masking excludes it instead of raising it to the lower bound.

fields.question: Which PPO gradients does GPPO recover?
fields.answer: Ordinary clipping can stop gradients for positive-advantage high ratios and negative-advantage low ratios. GPPO restores backward signal while keeping the forward value.
fields.example: A bad action already made rarer may still need an avoidance gradient.

fields.question: Why can identical forward losses produce different updates?
fields.answer: Stop-gradient can change derivatives without changing values. GPPO separates forward and backward, so scalar logs cannot verify it.
fields.example: Two functions with equal output can have different derivatives through detach.

fields.question: Is equality of clipped GPPO/PPO loss values enough to test implementation?
fields.answer: No. Verify gradients in out-of-bound advantage quadrants against PPO's zero gradients, and explicit detach boundaries. No paper-scale long-CoT training.
fields.example: Positive advantage and a ratio above the upper bound directly test the recovered path.

fields.question: Why can GPPO have PPO-like forward values and nonzero clipped-region gradients?
fields.answer: Stop-gradient constructions decouple clipping values and derivatives. Boundary weights restore learning in flattened quadrants for positive exploration and negative examples. Inspect gradients, not just loss.
fields.example: Two operators can print one clipped score but only one has a boundary-weighted derivative.

fields.question: Why use TIS for equal-weight training and inference engines?
fields.answer: Precision and kernels can change probabilities, so rollout and training rescoring distributions differ. The ratio corrects implementation mismatch, not task rewards.
fields.example: Two compute paths using identical weights can assign slightly different token likelihoods.

fields.question: Why does TIS upper-clip instead of two-sided dropping like IcePop?
fields.answer: Capping large weights controls heavy tails while retaining small contributions. Two-sided masking drops severe mismatch in either direction. Zeroing small TIS weights changes the method.
fields.example: A tiny TIS ratio still contributes a little.

fields.question: Which probability is the TIS denominator?
fields.answer: Use the actual rollout engine probability below corresponding training probability; a separate policy ratio may follow. Local deterministic perturbations aren't vLLM/FSDP validation.
fields.example: Reversing the ratio can upweight an example that should be downweighted.

fields.question: Why upper-clip engine ratios but keep small weights in TIS?
fields.answer: Correction targets the training distribution. Huge weights can dominate variance; cap them. Small ratios indicate smaller target contributions, not automatic invalidity. This is not PPO policy ratio or two-sided masking.
fields.example: A token common in rollout but rare in training should contribute less without necessarily being removed.
